title: Sort Items by Groups Respecting Dependencies
statement:
You have `n` items numbered `0` to `n - 1` and `m` groups numbered `0` to `m - 1`. Item `i` is in group `group[i]`, or in no group when `group[i]` is `-1`; some groups may have no items at all. The list `beforeItems[i]` names every item that has to appear somewhere to the left of item `i`.

Return an arrangement of all `n` items that satisfies both rules:

- every item listed in `beforeItems[i]` is placed earlier than item `i`;
- the items that share a group sit together as one unbroken run (items with group `-1` are free of this rule).

When several arrangements work, any one of them is accepted. When none exists, return an empty list.
signature: int[] sortItems(int n, int m, int[] group, List<List<Integer>> beforeItems)
notes:
## Intuition

Two kinds of order are mixed together. Inside a group, items must follow their own dependencies. Between groups, a rule from an item of group A to an item of group B forces the whole block A to come before block B. So build **two** dependency graphs, one over items and one over groups, and topologically sort each. If either graph has a cycle, no arrangement exists. Trying every permutation would also work, but only for a handful of items.

## Approach

1. Copy `group` into `groupOf` and give every ungrouped item its own new group id, so each item belongs to exactly one group. `groupCount` ends as the total number of groups.
2. For every rule `before -> item`, add an edge in the item graph. If the two items are in different groups, also add the edge `groupOf[before] -> groupOf[item]` in the group graph.
3. Run Kahn's algorithm (`topologicalOrder`) on both graphs. A shorter order than the node count means a cycle, so return `[]`.
4. Walk `itemOrder` and drop each item into `members` of its group; each bucket stays in a valid order.
5. Walk `groupOrder` and append each group's `members` to `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

Items 0, 1 and 7 get the new groups 2, 3 and 4, so `groupOf = [2, 3, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 4]`. The rules give the item edges 6->1, 5->2, 6->3, 3->4, 6->4 and the group edges 0->3 (from 6->1). The item order is `[0, 5, 6, 7, 2, 1, 3, 4]` and the group order is `[0, 1, 2, 4, 3]`. Group 0 holds `[6, 3, 4]`, group 1 holds `[5, 2]`, then `[0]`, `[7]`, `[1]`, giving `[6, 3, 4, 5, 2, 0, 7, 1]`, a valid arrangement.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + m + E), where E is the total length of `beforeItems`: each graph is built and sorted with every node and edge handled once.
- Space: O(n + m + E) for the two graphs, their in-degrees and the buckets.

## Pitfalls

- Ungrouped items must not all share group `-1`; each needs its own group, or they would be forced together.
- A rule between two items of the same group adds no group edge; adding one would create a self-loop and a false cycle.
- Sorting the items alone is not enough: `[0, -1, 0]` with rules 0->1->2 has no cycle among items, yet group 0 cannot stay together.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `groupOf` | group of each item, with fresh ids for ungrouped items |
| `groupCount` | number of groups after the fresh ids |
| `itemNext`, `itemIndegree` | item graph edges and in-degrees |
| `groupNext`, `groupIndegree` | group graph edges and in-degrees |
| `itemOrder`, `groupOrder` | topological orders of items and groups |
| `members` | items of each group in item order |
| `id`, `result` | the group being appended, and the arrangement built so far |
| `order`, `head` | Kahn's queue and its read position |
